**Rounds 31-32 (2026-09-02/03) — consensus reached, invalidated by my own
template, and the Windows question settled by ruling.** Round 31 produced
the first simultaneous PASS in this panel's history: Anthropic PASS (two
Minors, both already-disclosed open work) and Codex PASS (three Minors) on
one digest. The aggregation then rejected the Codex verdict: my
reconstructed runner template had omitted the `blind: true` attestation the
aggregator requires. I did not add the field to the panelist's verdict
myself — editing panel evidence post-hoc is not mine to do — and re-ran the
Codex slot on the SAME digest with the corrected template.

The re-run returned NEEDS_WORK with a Major the previous run had not raised:
`_fsync_directory` is POSIX-only, so Windows lacks every directory-entry
durability barrier while AC-047 carries no platform qualifier. Identical
bytes, same vendor, PASS then Major — the WFI-060 nondeterminism, now
demonstrated within one slot. The finding itself is factually right and has
been disclosed since round 24; Python has no portable Windows
directory-synchronization primitive, and a ctypes mechanism would ship
untested from this environment. Put to the owner with three options; the
owner ruled 「裁定で閉じる（推奨）」 (2026-09-03). Ruling (B) in
investigation.md records the scope verbatim: the barriers are POSIX-only by
design, Windows retains the pre-round-19 posture every platform once had,
the exposure is stated rather than buried, and a tested Windows barrier is
future work, not a defect of this task. The `_fsync_directory` docstring
cites the ruling so the panel sees the adjudication in the code it reviews.

**Round 30 (2026-09-02) — the barrier generalized to the principle, and the
enumeration my own count bump left behind.**

The OpenAI Major generalized its own round-29 finding one step further, and
rightly: the round-29 barrier fsynced only resolver-evidence.yaml's parent
before a recovery discard, and the Context Projection lives under a
DIFFERENT parent — so a rollback restore whose own barrier had failed could
still present a volatile PRE, be accepted, and have its journal durably
deleted; a later crash would resurrect the POST entry with no journal left.
The scan now fsyncs EVERY distinct parent named by the journal before ANY
discard it performs, failing closed on the existing diagnostic. That is the
principle itself rather than another special case, which is what closes this
axis: rounds 26, 29 and 30 were each the same lesson at wider scope, and
there is no wider scope left than "every entry".

The Anthropic Majors were the enumeration class again, in its purest form:
my round-29 edit bumped 「残る 3 件」 to 「残る 4 件」 and left the
parenthetical at （F と O） — four claimed, two named, in the very passage
that narrates fixing this class. The contract's comment likewise still said
"Both remaining uncovered guards". Where a list can be replaced by a
pointer to the authority it now is ("whatever this log ends with"), it was;
where a list must stand, it names all four.

Mutant T's anchor died in the generalization (the uniqueness assert caught
it before a silent no-op, again) and is rebound to the parent-directory
loop; S still kills at 393/2, T remains uncovered with its two-fault
obstacle stated.

**Round 29 (2026-09-02) — my round-26 insurance, cancelled by my round-28
convergence; and the verifier's blind spots, mapped by both slots at once.**

The OpenAI Major was an interaction between two of my own fixes. Round 26
retains the journal when a Block record's directory barrier fails —
`wrote=False`, the journal is that record's backstop. Round 28 taught the
recovery scan to converge exactly that batch shape — and its discard deleted
the backstop without ever establishing the durability whose absence was the
reason the journal existed. A crash after that cleanup could lose the
not-yet-durable Block record with no journal left to expose it. The scan now
re-runs the Evidence directory barrier BEFORE the discard, and a failure
keeps the journal on the existing diagnostic rather than trading a durable
record for a tidy staging area. Mutant U-candidate disclosed as T:
observing the revert needs two fault conditions in one run (a failed fsync
inside a scan already converging a retained journal), beyond the single-shot
overlays — a measured obstacle, recorded as open work, not an impossibility
claim; four of those were offered here (C, D, M, O) and all four were wrong.

The Anthropic slot returned three Majors, all count drift, and named the
uncomfortable fact directly: the verifier written in response to round 25
did not catch them. Both causes were mine. The verifier scanned only the
report's head — everything before the FIRST round entry — while the live
Test Result field, the regression table and half of Files Changed sit BELOW
the round history in this document. And its exemption looked at the line
above as well as the line itself, so round 25's own correction note
("historical, all superseded") shielded the live, wrong figure in the next
sentence. The verifier now scans the whole report and a marker only exempts
the number it sits with; re-run, it re-found all three panel sites
independently before any were fixed, plus the historical quotations, which
now carry explicit same-line markers instead of relying on proximity.

**Round 28 (2026-09-02) — the first PASS from one slot, and a transient
error that had been made permanent.** The Anthropic slot returned PASS (no
Critical, no Major, four Minor) after measuring every figure itself and
crediting none from the briefing: it recounted the regression at 631, and
confirmed the round-27 manifest binding by matching the manifest row, the
mutation log's `restored sha256`, and the Outputs declaration against each
other.

The OpenAI Major was the sharpest correctness finding since the staging
chain. A Block that FOLLOWS a completed rollback leaves the publication
artifacts at PRE and Evidence holding the BLOCK RECORD — which is, by
construction, neither the PRE bytes nor the POST bytes that journal
recorded, because REQ-001 step (m) makes Evidence the explicit non-subject
of the rollback so that record survives it. The recovery scan classified
that as the unrecoverable third state. So if the journal's unlink failed at
that instant — an ordinary transient error — every future invocation would
Block forever on a batch whose rollback had in fact completed correctly, and
the report's claim that the next scan retries the discard was false for
precisely this shape. Evidence now has its own branch, safe ONLY when every
other entry is at PRE; mixed with any POST artifact the state is unexplained
again and fails closed on the same diagnostic. A planted-journal fixture
reproduces the exact shape and asserts the scan converges and discards;
mutant S removes the branch and dies at 393/2.

The Anthropic Minor worth acting on was that round 27's source scan read
only the Python master while this task's sibling scan already treats the
Resolver as all three of py/sh/ps1 — the class was closed for a third of the
surface. The scan now reads all three.

**Round 27 (2026-09-02) — a manifest that no longer bound the bytes it
names, and a diagnostic line no fixture could see.**

The Anthropic slot's Critical was the sharpest artifact finding of this
package: `MANIFEST.sha256` still carried the round-25 hash for the Python
master while the Outputs table and the mutation log carried the round-26 one.
The slot checked the alternative reading — manifest fresh, everything else
stale — by hashing the manifest's own bytes inside the bundle and matching
them against the Outputs row that declares them, proving both sides current
and the mismatch real. `shasum -a 256 -c` was 3/4 with one FAILED while this
report asserted 4/4 OK in three places, and that manifest is what gates the
human apply route.

The cause was procedural: round 26 changed the resolver, Outputs was
re-derived, and regenerating the manifest was a step I remembered on earlier
rounds and did not remember on that one. It is now a script that runs inside
every recapture, between the mutation pass (which restores the resolver) and
the gates, and it refuses to write a manifest whose ROW COUNT changed --
because a manifest that silently lost an entry would still verify clean.
`shasum -c` is now 4/4, exit 0, measured.

The OpenAI Major was the same round-21 addition seen from the other side.
That round's fix printed `capability-resolver: warning: ...` on a cleanup
failure, and `warning` is not one of REQ-002's sixteen diagnostic ids.
AC-014 binds EVERY diagnostic line the Resolver emits, while TEST-014's
runtime assertion only sees ids its own fixtures produce — so a line no
fixture drives was outside the only check that existed. The line is removed;
round 21's substantive fix was the return VALUE, which the two recovery-scan
callers check and halt on, and the stderr line was an addition beyond it.
TEST-014 now also scans the shipped source for every literal diagnostic
prefix it writes, comment mentions excluded, so the class is caught whether
or not a fixture reaches the line. Mutant R reinstates the removed line and
dies at 391/1, which is the proof that the new assertion is not vacuous.

**Round 26 (2026-09-02) — the guard I hollowed out myself, and a correction
that made a right number wrong.** Both slots returned NEEDS_WORK on one
frozen digest.

The OpenAI Major was an internal contradiction I introduced on round 21.
`_write_evidence` caught `_ReplacedButNotDurable` — which means the Block
record's directory barrier FAILED — and returned normally, so
`_block_reporting` reported `wrote_evidence=True`, and `wrote` is exactly
what the three Block-after-rollback callers consult before discarding the
journal. A crash could then persist the journal's deletion while losing the
Block record's rename: artifacts back at PRE, no record, and no journal left
to expose it — the state the round-9 fix introduced that guard to prevent.
Round 21 had been answering a real Anthropic Minor (mapping it to "no live
rename had yet been committed" was untrue of the disk), but it answered with
the wrong branch. The exception now propagates and the caller emits the
canonical Block line while reporting `wrote=False`, so the record stands and
the journal is RETAINED. Mutant Q records the revert.

The Anthropic Majors were both in this report. Its Summary still opened by
asserting the architecture panel round 5 WITHDREW — that a Block's Evidence
goes through the journaled transaction — forty-five lines above the report's
own paragraph saying every such site had been corrected. And a bullet said
"eleven new fixture directories" against the thirteen its own Outputs table  <!-- historical: the value quoted here is the one being corrected -->
lists and its own next bullet states; that bullet no longer states a count at
all, because the count already lives one bullet below and duplicating it is
what produced the finding. The Minor: the Python master was described as
2,505 lines when it is over 3,500.

The most useful finding is one no panelist raised as a defect. The Anthropic
slot noted it did NOT credit the 681 figure my briefing gave for the sibling
suites, and enumerated 631 by hand. It was right: 631 is the sum of one
figure per suite, and 681 comes from summing every "N passed" match in the
log, which double-counts per-launcher lines. I had asserted 681 in a commit
message while calling the correct 631 "itself stale" — a correction that made
a right number wrong, which is the precise failure this package's verifier
exists to prevent, committed by the person maintaining the verifier. The
regression total is now part of the verifier's measured ground truth, and
computing it surfaced a second off-by-one: one suite ends with its own
`PASS: 20` summary line, so counting lines beginning with PASS counted the
summary as a 21st test. Machine measurement and the panel's hand enumeration
now agree at 631.

**Round 25 (2026-09-02) — the verifier that verified my memory instead of
the documents.** The Anthropic slot returned NEEDS_WORK with two Majors, both
count drift in declared outputs: the report stated `grep -c '^def
run_t007_'` reports **sixteen** where the shipped driver returns seventeen,  <!-- historical: the value quoted here is the one being corrected -->
and gave three different values for that one fact; the CHANGELOG entry
carried eleven fixture directories (thirteen) and `15 mutant 中 13 件`  <!-- historical: the value quoted here is the one being corrected -->
(sixteen, fourteen). Both understate coverage, so this is staleness rather
than fabrication -- but one was framed as a MEASUREMENT.

The count verifier had reported clean. It was blacklisting specific stale
strings (`reports **fifteen**`), so it went blind the moment a claim drifted
to a value the blacklist did not name: it verified my memory of past
mistakes, not the documents. It is rewritten to measure truth from the tree
and flag any claim of that KIND whose number differs. Two of its own defects
surfaced during the rewrite: the alternation was shortest-first, so `six`
matched inside `sixteen` and it read 16 as 6; and an exemption keyword
anywhere in a five-line window exempted that window's LIVE counts, which is
precisely how a paragraph discussing staleness protected its own stale
numbers. The rewritten verifier re-found all three panel sites independently
before any of them were fixed. The report passage that carried three
phrasings of one count now carries one, because a verifier can be taught one
phrasing at a time and cannot be taught all of them.

The two Minors: the staging-chain overlay's `_tracking_replace` arming was
dead code copied from its sibling, and is removed. Mutant O's note claimed
its barrier was unobservable in-process; a panelist refuted that with the
argument that had already killed the same claim for mutant M. Three fixture
attempts followed and all three were withdrawn -- arming on `_restore_to_pre`
alone fired on the NON-ABSENT branch's write-side fsync, excluding
`_atomic_write_bytes` then never fired, and removing a sentinel at
overlay-import time did not produce an ABSENT PRE either. The measured
obstacle is that `plant_sentinels` writes all three publication artifacts
before every fixture, so no rollback in this suite reaches the ABSENT branch
at all. The log now records that fact instead of an impossibility claim:
four such claims have been made here (C, D, M, O) and all four were wrong,
so a fifth is not offered.

Separately, this round's tooling was rebuilt after the scratchpad copies
vanished, and the first reconstruction was wrong -- it invoked gates with
`--feature` flags they do not take, called `check-risk-upgrade.sh` (a
different plugin's script with different output) instead of `check-risk.sh`,
and ran `check-workflow-state.sh` under dash, which dies at line 193. It
overwrote real evidence with exit 127 and five red gates before the exit
codes were read. The logs were restored from git and every invocation was
then determined by RUNNING each gate and reading its own usage. The bundle
build had also hung for 7.5 hours at 0.01s CPU: homebrew bash 5.3.9
deadlocks writing a here-document to a pipe, and the build completes
immediately under `/bin/bash`.

**Round 24 (2026-08-29) — one durability link above the last two, and a
fixture that had started passing for the wrong reason.** The Anthropic slot
did not run (vendor credit exhaustion); the OpenAI slot found a real Major.
Rounds 19-20 fsynced the directories the published FILES live in, but the
batch directory's own entry lives in `.resolver-staging`, and that directory's
entry lives in `specs/<feature>`. Neither was fsynced, so a power loss could
persist a fsynced live rename and lose the nonce directory carrying the
journal: a partial publication with no journal for the recovery scan to find,
which is the one shape REQ-001/AC-047 exist to forbid. Both links are now
fsynced before the journal write, and therefore before any live rename. The
three directory-fsync sites became one `_fsync_directory` helper.

This time the fix shipped WITH its fixture, and writing it paid for itself
three times over:

1. The new barrier broke the round-22 `publication-fsync-failure` case,
   because the staging-chain fsync became the first feature-directory fsync
   and the injection fired there instead. The overlay now arms only after a
   rename lands, so the two fixtures separate the two barriers cleanly.
2. Collapsing the fsync sites invalidated mutants M and O's anchors, and the
   uniqueness assert halted instead of silently mutating nothing — the third
   time that guard has prevented a false UNCOVERED row.
3. Mutant M's tally then fell from killed to control, and the reason was not
   the refactor. A stack-trace probe showed the injected failure firing at
   the FILE fsync inside `_atomic_write_bytes`: the overlay had been keeping
   CLOSED directory descriptor numbers in its watch set, and the kernel
   reused one for a temp file. The case had been passing while exercising a
   different barrier than its name claims — a test that had quietly stopped
   testing its subject. The overlay now discards descriptors on close, and
   under mutant M the injection provably never fires at all.

Mutant P (both staging-chain fsync calls removed) is killed by the new
`publication-staging-chain-fsync-failure` case, which asserts the ZERO-rename
clause that a pre-journal barrier failure must produce.

**Round 23 (2026-08-29) — the return value I consumed at one call site out
of three, and the sweep that finally became a check.** The panel split once
more on the same digest: the Anthropic slot PASSED (three prose-count
Minors), the OpenAI slot found a real Major. Round 21 gave `_discard_batch`
a return value and consumed it only at the success-path Complete. Both
recovery-scan discard sites ignored a failed cleanup and let the run proceed
into a fresh resolve — and a stale journal surviving past the scan is the
one thing the scan exists to prevent, because step 14 then publishes new
bytes, the journal's recorded targets match neither PRE nor POST, and a
journal that was SAFELY convergeable this run becomes unrecoverable the
next. Both sites now halt on a failed discard with the existing
`publication-journal-recovery` id. The other unchecked call sites (the
zero-commit rollback discard and the three Block-path deferred discards)
are safe by ordering, not by luck: each is followed by the run ENDING, so
the next invocation's scan retries the discard before any new publication
can re-stale the journal — Codex's precision in naming exactly the two
dangerous sites was correct.

The Anthropic Minors were more stale prose counts, and they exposed that
the round-22 verifier's patterns were too narrow (slash-form tallies only,
backtick-adjacent names only). The verifier now matches comma-form tallies
and bare word-counts, exempts labelled historical records by their own
markers, and passed clean before this commit — the second commit it has
gated.

**Round 19 (2026-08-29) — ruling (A), and retiring a guard that was wrong in
both directions.**

The Anthropic slot's two round-18 Majors were both about round 17's
read-containment clause, and both were right.

It was under-scoped as a READ guard. The boundary
`requirements.md:1304-1311` states is "never ... reads a credential", not
"never reads outside the repository" — so a publication target symlinked to an
in-repo `.env` or a token-bearing git config passed it, had its bytes captured
into the PRE image, and on the rollback path the suite itself exercises, those
bytes were written into a git-tracked artifact path. The round-15 fixture used
an in-feature referent and the round-17 fixture an out-of-repo one; the whole
middle band was unguarded and untested.

It was also over-applied as a WRITE guard. `_write_evidence` consults the same
predicate before a direct temp+fsync+rename that performs no read at all, so
the clause bought nothing there and cost the Block record — silently widening
the owner-ruled THIRD AC-012 no-write exception to a FOURTH condition,
disclosed nowhere and covered by nothing.

The owner ruled **(A)**: a publication target that is a symlink is never read
through, and its PRE state is `ABSENT`. That moves the rule to where the read
happens — `_live_bytes` — and it holds identically at all four of its call
sites (PRE capture, rollback verification, recovery classification,
post-restore verification), because "a symlink is not this artifact's content"
is one reading, not four. The round-17 clause is retired in both directions
and `_target_escapes_via_symlink` is back to meaning only what its name says:
where a write lands.

**The accepted consequence, asserted rather than glossed.** Under (A) a
rollback restores `ABSENT` by unlinking, so a symlinked target does not
survive a rolled-back publication. The round-15 fixture's assertion that the
lexical entry holds its PRE bytes therefore stopped holding. It was rewritten
to the property (A) does guarantee, not deleted — deleting an assertion
because its old form broke would have thrown away the only check watching that
path — and a third assertion was added for the band the repository-containment
check missed: the referent's bytes are captured nowhere, for an IN-TREE
referent.

Mutant K now mutates `_live_bytes` back to following the leaf and is killed
(380/3 at the round-19 capture; the current figure is whatever `mutation-proofs.log` carries — a fixed number here went stale twice).

**Round 16 (2026-08-29) — the owner's ruling (c), the third-branch sweep, and
a mutation that was testing the wrong line.**

The owner was given the state after fifteen rounds and answered
「君の推奨案で進めろ」 to a recommendation of: issue a scope ruling, and raise
the panel rule itself as a WFI. Both are recorded in `investigation.md` under
Ruling (c), with the counter-argument stated rather than omitted — deletion of
an in-set artifact is more destructive than the substitution round 1 ruled out
of scope, and the ruling was made in full view of that.

The ruling covers attacker-driven journal manipulation only, so the two
round-15 findings outside that class were handled on their merits rather than
swept up by it. The `artifact-publication-failed` branch discarded its journal
before the Block record was durable — the same defect already fixed on the two
post-publication branches, so it is fixed here too: the exception carries its
transaction and rollback outcome, and the caller discards only once
`_block_reporting` confirms the write. All three Block-after-rollback paths
now share one discard discipline. The all-POST recovery classification is the
frozen four-outcome contract behaving as specified; changing it is a contract
change, so it is recorded as a known limitation instead.

**And that sweep silently broke a mutant.** Adding `discard=False` to
`_publish_bundle` made mutant C's anchor string match two call sites, so a
first-match replace began mutating `_publish_bundle` instead of the
post-publication branch. The suite stayed green and the mutation reported
UNCOVERED — a mutant that appears to prove something while testing a line no
fixture exercises. Caught only because mutant C had been killing at 368/1 the
round before and suddenly was not. The anchor is now the three-line
post-publication call, and the script asserts the anchor occurs exactly once,
so the next ambiguity stops the run instead of producing a false negative.

Verified after the fix: mutant C back to 368/1, every other mutant byte-for-byte
unchanged (A 368/1, B 366/3, D 369/0, E 366/3, F 369/0, G 365/4) — so the
third-branch sweep cost no existing coverage.

**Round 15 (2026-08-29) — both open findings closed with fixtures, and one
of my own disclosures shown to be false.**

The OpenAI slot's Major was real, and worse than a shape complaint.
`_recover_journal` checked that every journal entry named an in-set path and
that no path repeated, but never that the SET was a bundle this Resolver
could have written. An attacker-committed journal naming
`{facet-manifest, capability-summary}` — both genuinely in-set — with
`pre_hash: "ABSENT"` on the first and its real live hash as `post_hash`
classifies that live artifact as committed, forces MIX with the second entry,
and the rollback UNLINKS a file that was never part of any transaction.
`_legitimate_journal_bundles` now requires the set to be the Full track's
three targets or the Lite track's two. `run_t007_journal_bundle_shape_case`
plants exactly that journal and asserts, above all, that
`facet-manifest.yaml` is still there. Mutant G removes the check and kills the
case on four assertions — so the finding was a live defect, not a
theoretical one.

Writing it surfaced a second defect of mine that no test could have caught:
the check read `if seen_paths not in _legitimate_journal_bundles(...)`, and
`seen_paths` is a `set`, which is unhashable — membership would have raised
`TypeError` on the first legitimate journal. The suite stayed green because
no fixture reached that line at the moment it was written. `frozenset(...)`
now wraps it.

**The Anthropic slot was right that mutant C was reachable, and my
disclosure was wrong.** Round 9 said no fixture could observe the
crash window "without a new test-harness kill hook between the rollback and
the Evidence write"; the slot answered that the hook already exists and its
kill point is one integer. It does.
`post-publication-crash-before-evidence/registry_discovery.py` kills before
the SECOND rename to `resolver-evidence.yaml` — the first being the commit's,
the second the Block record's — which is exactly that window.
`run_t007_crash_before_evidence_case` asserts the journal is still standing at
that instant, and mutant C now dies. **At round 15, uncovered guards dropped
from three to two** (D and F). **Round 19 corrects the current value to one:
F and O are the uncovered pair (this sentence has now been corrected three times — only-F, then F-and-M, now F-and-O — as round 22's fault-injection fixture killed M and added O; the recurring lesson is that a count in prose is a claim with a shelf life); D is covered by `nonce-names-another-batch`, M by `publication-fsync-failure`.**

One prediction of mine failed while writing it, and the test records why
rather than hiding it: I expected the next invocation to Block
`publication-journal-recovery`. It converges the journal instead, which is
correct — the crashed run had already rolled its artifacts back, so the scan
can finish the job. The assertion was rewritten to the property that actually
holds, with that reasoning kept beside it.

`t007_install_fixture` gained the ability to install both overlays at once
(a `resolve-component-paths.py` subprocess stub to steer the branch, and a
`registry_discovery.py` in-process kill hook to crash inside it). Neither

**Round 13 (2026-08-29) — the round-9 guard was on the wrong predicate.**
The OpenAI slot found that both post-publication branches discarded the
retained journal whenever `complete` was true, and `complete` says only that
the ROLLBACK finished. `_block` swallows both of its write-failure conditions
into `_block_no_write` and returns a bare exit code, so the caller could not
tell whether the Block record had actually reached Evidence's live path. The
journal was therefore deleted even when the Evidence write had failed —
precisely the state round 9's deferral existed to prevent: artifacts back at
PRE, the success-form Evidence still live from the commit, and no journal for
the recovery scan to find.

`_block`'s body moved to `_block_reporting`, which returns
`(exit_code, wrote_evidence)`; `_block` is now a thin wrapper returning the
code, so all forty of its call sites are untouched. The two post-publication
branches call `_block_reporting` and discard only when `complete and wrote`.

**This paragraph's claim that D was unreachable was wrong when written.**
Round 15 covered C, and round 19's `nonce-names-another-batch` fixture covers D;
the current uncovered set has **one** mutant, F. The branch represented by F
cannot be reached by a fixture: reaching it needs the Evidence write to fail
AFTER a completed rollback, and the two conditions are mutually exclusive in
any fixture because a feature directory malformed enough to make the Evidence
target uncontained also makes the publication targets uncontained, so the
publish is refused before any commit happens. Mutant F records it, and
the OpenAI slot said the same thing independently — its finding notes that
neither the disclosed `ArtifactPublicationFailed` branch nor the mutant-C gap
exercises this combination.

**A pattern worth carrying to the retrospective rather than hiding.** Five
consecutive panel rounds have produced a finding on this one code path — the
relationship between the rollback, the Block Evidence write, and the
journal's lifetime. Every fix was correct and each finding was narrower than
the last. Its claim that three resulting guards were unreachable was wrong;
the current value is **one**, mutant F. Whether that sequence is converging
because the code is right, or because the panel has exhausted the angles it can see, is not
something this report can settle from the inside. What is certain is that
this area's correctness rests more on review than on tests, and a future
change here has no regression net for that **one** guard, F.

**Round 12 (2026-08-28) — ruling (b)'s own defect, and the fixture that
should have existed before it.** Both slots returned a Major on the round-11
bytes and both were real.

The OpenAI slot found the one that mattered. Ruling (b) made a symlink AT a
publication target's leaf acceptable, which is right for the write — but
`_repo_relative` resolves the whole path, so the journal then recorded the
symlink's REFERENT while the commit replaced the LEXICAL entry. Rollback and
crash recovery both work from the recorded path, so they restored the
referent and left the entry the commit actually wrote still holding its POST
bytes: a rollback that reports success and did not undo the publication.
`_repo_relative_target` now records the lexical entry, by the same
parent-resolve rule the containment check uses. A check and a journal that
disagree about what "the target" means reintroduce exactly this class, so the
two must stay on one rule.

**This time the answer was a fixture, not a fourth disclosure.** Two
consecutive rounds produced Majors reachable only through a branch no test
entered. `run_t007_leaf_symlink_target_case` runs the
post-publication-mismatch path — the only path where a completed commit is
rolled back and the outcome stays observable — with `facet-manifest.yaml`
planted as a symlink to an in-tree sibling. Five assertions: the publish is
not refused, the LEXICAL entry holds its PRE bytes after rollback, the
referent is byte-untouched, and no journal or staging litter survives. The
load-bearing one is the lexical entry: restoring the referent instead is
invisible there, because the referent already holds the PRE bytes and a
rollback would rewrite them unchanged and report complete. Mutant E kills it
on three assertions, and mutant B now kills on three as well.

The Anthropic slot's Major landed on the contract, and it was the same
propagation class a twelfth time — this time on the artifact that declares
two required checks passed. `T-007.contract.json` said `355/0` twice while
its own declared captures said `356/0`, and cited a non-existent
`mutation-proofs-test059.log`. Round 11 had carried 356 into this report and
`investigation.md` and left the contract and `CHANGELOG.md` behind.

Two structural fixes, so this stops recurring on these artifacts. The
mutation log is renamed `mutation-proofs.log` — a name with a round number in
it is guaranteed to go stale, and that name was already wrong for a log
carrying five mutants from four rounds. And the contract now states the green
tally ONCE, saying in the comment itself why: it came to disagree with its own
evidence by restating the number in a second place.

Repairing that contract also surfaced a defect of mine that no gate had
caught: **it had been invalid JSON since round 8**, because I wrote raw `"`
quotes inside the comment string and never re-ran `check-contract` afterwards.
Nothing flagged it, because a contract is only validated for tasks already at

**Round 11 (2026-08-28) — the owner ruled, and both halves of the standing
Major are now closed.** The question left open at the end of round 10 was put
to the repository owner, who answered 「(a) 受容 / (b) 承認」.

Ruling (b) narrows `_target_escapes_via_symlink` to resolve the target's
PARENT and join the leaf on by name. Every write in this file lands via
`os.replace(tmp, target)`, which replaces the directory entry at `target`
rather than following a symlink sitting there, and the temp file is created
with `mkstemp(dir=target.parent)` — so the parent is the only component whose
symlinks can move a write, and resolving the leaf as well modelled a write
this code does not perform. What is still caught is unchanged in substance: a
symlinked `specs/<feature>`, a symlinked `generated/`, any symlink between
the trusted base and the parent, and every lexical `..` traversal. Reading is
the one operation that does follow a leaf symlink (`_live_bytes` captures the
PRE image) and it cannot escape either, because a rollback writes those bytes
back to the leaf NAME inside the tree, never to the symlink's own target.

Ruling (a) accepts `EvidenceTargetUncontained` as a third AC-012 no-write
exception, a known limitation rather than an open defect. **No frozen
document was amended for it.** The ruling is recorded in the exception's own
docstring and in `investigation.md` — the same way the 2026-08-27 ruling on
the doubly-degraded rollback corner was recorded — because amending
`requirements.md` line 386 would invalidate all three currently-green review
gates and force the whole spec → impl → task chain again for a single count.

The two rulings interact, and that is why (b) was worth taking: it shrinks
(a)'s reach to the irreducible case. A symlink at `resolver-evidence.yaml`
itself no longer suppresses Evidence; what remains is a feature directory
that genuinely resolves outside the tree, where no valid write exists at all.

Both edits were behaviour-preserving against the suite as it then stood
(356/0 in both runtimes, unchanged by either). That was not reassurance but
the warning, and round 12 below is what it warned about: no fixture placed a
symlink at a leaf publication target, so ruling (b)'s newly-permitted branch
was entirely unexercised.

`specs/epic-193-a5-capability-resolver/investigation.md` is touched by this
round but is NOT listed in the Outputs table above, for the same reason
`tasks.md` is not: it is a feature-level record this task amends, not an
artifact this task authors. It reaches the panel anyway — the bundle carries
it as one of the feature's spec documents — so the rulings are visible to
every reviewer without being double-declared here.

**Still open, and not an implementer's call.** The OpenAI Major has two
halves. Its first is the `EvidenceTargetUncontained` third AC-012 no-write
exception, escalated for a ruling and unresolved: `requirements.md` line 386
says the always-emitted rule "excepts exactly two diagnostic ids", and when a

is no third option — writing violates containment, not writing violates

### ps1 / sh twin disclosure

The `.sh` and `.ps1` twins are **thin dispatchers**, not ports: each is a
frozen T-002/T-004 launcher whose only job is to locate a Python interpreter
and `exec`/`Start-Process` the Python master ("Thin POSIX dispatcher; the
Python master is the sole implementation."). There is therefore no
mechanism-level twin to keep in sync for this task, and neither file needed a
byte of change -- their manifest hashes are unchanged
(`03986de0...` / `d8eb9429...`). This is the architecture T-004 already froze,
not a divergence this task introduced; `RESOLVER_VERSION` and every rule live
in the master precisely so `.py`/`.sh`/`.ps1` parity (REQ-005/AC-023) is
structural.

`pwsh` genuinely executed everything on this Mac (`pwsh 7.6.2`,
`[PATH_REDACTED]). The ps1 paths executed locally were:
`tests/resolve-project-context-block.tests.ps1` (RED 272/23 and round-1 GREEN 306/0 — the shipped GREEN is `green-shipped-ps1.log` at the tally the contract states,
each capture led by its own `# runner: pwsh` marker line, which the suite emits
specifically so a ps1 capture cannot be a duplicated sh capture), plus
`resolve-project-context-{match,cli,discovery,lite}.tests.ps1`. Each of those
runs drives the resolver through
`pwsh -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .../resolve-project-context.ps1`
for every fixture (the driver's own `launcher_args`), so the `.ps1` dispatcher
itself is executed once per invocation in that lane -- including the crashed
invocations, whose kill hook fires inside the Python child the `.ps1`
dispatcher started, and whose non-zero exit the dispatcher propagates.

## Specification Differences

None. The implementation follows the frozen contract; the four decision points
that required reading two clauses together are recorded here so a reviewer can
check the reasoning rather than re-derive it:

1. **Block-path Evidence is written DIRECTLY, not through the transaction**
   (rewritten 2026-08-28; the earlier text asserted the opposite and was the
   withdrawn route). design.md:1208-1210 ("... or (on any Block reached at
   step 1/9/10/12/13, above) Resolver Evidence alone, is published via that
   journaled transaction") and design.md:1261-1262 ("exactly one target ...
   on a Block") do say what they say, and `_write_evidence` was originally
   rerouted onto `_publish_bundle` because of them. Panel round 5 established
   that those two sentences are the stale siblings: design.md:1419 and :2846
   require the Block's Evidence write to be a direct `temp file + fsync +
   rename` with "no staging area, no journal", and requirements.md line 371
   says it verbatim ("published directly, not through the journaled
   transaction"). Three sites against two, with the two carrying the explicit
   reasoning (a one-file write needs no cross-file atomicity; opening a second
   journal against a Feature whose journal this invocation just declared
   unconvergeable is incoherent). The shipped code follows the three, and
   `_publish_and_complete` — the one-target helper the withdrawn reroute
   needed — was deleted as dead code once nothing called it.
2. **`publication-journal-recovery` still writes Resolver Evidence.**
   design.md's recovery clause says the Block leaves "the live state exactly
   as found", while REQ-002 (requirements.md:383-388) closes the
   Evidence-always rule at exactly two named exceptions, neither of which is
   this row, and AC-012 requires every TEST-010 fixture except those two to
   write a full record. The ACs settle it: Evidence is written, and the scan
   performs no PARTIAL recovery -- it pre-validates every backup before its
   first restore, and the journal and backups are retained for the operator.
   **Correction (panel round 3, Minor 1):** an earlier revision of this item
   also claimed "live state exactly as found" is honoured for "the journal's
   own targets". That is not strictly true. `resolver-evidence.yaml` is
   itself one of the four allowlisted targets a retained journal may list, so
   writing the AC-012-mandated Block record moves that target off both its
   recorded PRE and POST hashes -- which can convert an operator-fixable
   batch into an unconvergeable one (the same interaction the 2026-08-27
   ruling accepted as a known limitation). The Evidence write is defensible
   and disclosed; the over-broad "journal's own targets untouched" phrasing
   was the defect, and it is withdrawn here.
3. **A content-corrupted pre-image backup is unrecoverable.** design.md
   enumerates "missing or unreadable"; AC-047 requires the fixture that
   "corrupts the journal's own recorded pre-image backup" to Block. The
   implementation therefore also rejects a backup whose own hash no longer
   matches the journal's recorded PRE value -- strictly fail-closed, and the
   only reading under which AC-047's companion fixture can pass.
4. **A post-publication verification that cannot RUN is not a mismatch.**
   design.md defines the rollback for "any mismatch" and is silent on a
   verification dependency that fails to launch. Re-labelling such a failure
   `post-publication-generation-mismatch` is exactly the defect the
   cross-model panel rejected for step 13, and the diagnostic enum is closed
   at sixteen, so `_POST_PUBLICATION_DEPENDENCY_BLOCKS` rolls back identically
   and reuses the SAME id the corresponding step-13 handler already uses, with
   a `<detail>` naming the post-publication window. This branch has no fixture.
   The parenthetical claim that this task owned four fixtures was stale by the
   shipped bytes: the current value is **thirteen** fixture scenario directories,
   enumerated in this report's Outputs. The branch is documented in-code as
   defense-in-depth.

Two non-differences worth disclosing:

- **`specs/epic-193-a5-capability-resolver/tasks.md` shows as modified in
  `git status`, and this task did not touch it.** The working-tree copy
  (`83ce52fe029a4a5eb37fddc240812a878bca4eeec353cd4dae941e6342265015`)
  differs from the input manifest's declared hash
  (`6620f9f64f3625bff674bb8bc0a25c782c7111e8d01125fa42921c593bec9537`) by
  exactly one line -- T-007's own `Status: Planned` -> `Status: In Progress`
  lifecycle flip. `git show HEAD:...` hashes to the manifest's value, i.e. the
  manifest snapshot is HEAD and the flip is the orchestrator's own,
  pre-existing at this run's start. The T-007 block was read from the
  working-tree copy; nothing else in it differs.
- **The Python master is over 3,500 lines, far over the 500-line house guideline.**
  Splitting it would break the single-file staged-candidate contract every

  route) is built on, and is not in this task's scope.

## Quality Gate Focus

1. **Design fidelity of the four decision points above**, especially (1)
   routing Block-path Evidence through the transaction -- that is the change
   with the widest blast radius (every one of the 256 pre-existing checks
   exercises it) and the one most worth an independent read of
   design.md:1201-1226 and :1257-1262.
2. **The kill hook's placement.** It is a fixture-supplied
   `registry_discovery.py` overlay that installs a `sys.addaudithook`
   observer of the `os.rename` audit event and calls `os._exit(137)` on the
   second live-target rename. It is in a fixture because tasks.md's own
   Breaking API line forbids a new CLI flag (closing off Epic A1's own
   `--simulate-crash-after` shape) and security-spec.md's Secrets Management
   section forbids reading an environment variable. No shipped byte knows the
   hook exists. Worth confirming the reviewer agrees this is a fixture, not a
   production backdoor.
3. **The rollback-content assertions** (`== PRE bytes`, not `not exists()`)
   are the only thing separating a journal-based rollback from a bare
   `unlink`; mutation (a) is their non-vacuity proof.
4. **`run_block_matrix_completeness_check` runs last on purpose** -- it
   consumes ids recorded during the run. If a reviewer reorders `main()`, that
   check silently weakens.
5. **`artifact-publication-failed`'s injection is structural, not
   permission-based** (the Context Projection target's parent directory is
   replaced by a regular file, so `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` fails
   for every OS and every privilege level). A `chmod 0555` injection would
   silently do nothing when CI runs as root.

## Panel Round 1 Remediation (2026-08-27)

Blind cross-model panel: openai NEEDS_WORK, anthropic PASS-with-a-Minor (both
independently flagged the same second interaction). Every finding was verified
against the code before any change.

### MAJOR 1 — journal-directed writes outside the fixed target set: **REAL, and exploitable**

Verified, not merely accepted. `_recover_journal` resolved each recorded
`live_path` through `_journal_target_path` (`repo_root / candidate`, or the
candidate as-is when absolute) and handed it straight to `_restore_to_pre`,
which either `_atomic_write_bytes`es an attacker-supplied `pre/` backup onto it
or `unlink`s it (`pre_hash: "ABSENT"`). No containment check of any kind. The
journal lives in `specs/<feature>/.resolver-staging/`, which infra-spec.md
itself classifies as an unprotected repository-local staging area — so a
malicious branch can simply commit one.

The RED run (`red-panel1-sh.log`) demonstrates the exploit rather than
asserting it abstractly:

- `relative-traversal-write`: the victim file's content after the run was
  `b'ATTACKER-RESTORED\n'` — arbitrary content written to
  `<repo>/outside-target.txt` via `specs/example-feature/../../outside-target.txt`.
  Note this path never leaves the repository, so a repository-containment
  check ALONE would not have caught it.
- `absolute-path-unlink`: the victim file was `b'<MISSING>'` — arbitrary file
  deletion, driven by an absolute `live_path` with `pre_hash: "ABSENT"`.
- In both, the invocation then continued to `exit 0` with empty stderr: the
  attack was silent.

**Fix.** `_allowed_publication_targets(repo_root, feature)` is now the single
source of truth for this feature's entire live write set, transcribed from
requirements.md:1144-1151 (which fixes it by name) and security-spec.md's B2
destination column. `_recover_journal` validates EVERY entry against it — and
rejects duplicate live paths — before touching a single file, raising
`PublicationJournalUnrecoverable` (canonical `publication-journal-recovery`
line, no journal content interpolated into the detail). `_publish_bundle`
asserts its own constructed targets against the same set, so the write side
and the recovery side cannot drift apart. Comparison is by lexical
`os.path.normpath(os.path.abspath(...))`, deliberately not `Path.resolve()`:
resolving would follow symlinks on both sides, so a symlinked in-set path
pointing outside would compare equal and pass. The symlink case is closed
separately by the primitives themselves (`os.replace` replaces a symlink
rather than writing through it; `unlink` removes the link, not its referent).

New fixture `publication-journal-target-escape`, two scenarios (one per write
primitive), asserting the Block, the byte-untouched victim, the untouched
in-set targets (the refusal precedes any write), the retained journal, and the
exact Evidence record.

### MAJOR 2 — retained-journal / Block-Evidence interaction: **REAL as described; mechanism fix ESCALATED, wording corrected**

Verified by tracing: on an incomplete in-process rollback the journal is
retained, `main()` then returns through `_block` → `_write_evidence`, which
publishes `resolver-evidence.yaml` — itself one of the retained journal's
recorded targets. That target then matches neither its recorded PRE nor POST
hash, which `_recover_journal` classifies as the unrecoverable third state, so
the next invocation Blocks `publication-journal-recovery` for manual
intervention instead of converging. The panel is right that the claim was
stronger than the behavior.

Per the coordinator's option (b), the mechanism change is **not** being made
here, because the frozen contract forecloses every consistent option. Two
frozen mandates collide:

> requirements.md REQ-002, `artifact-publication-failed` row: "a rollback
> failure, if the in-process attempt cannot itself fully complete, is recorded
> in this same diagnostic's own `detail` and safely completed by the next
> invocation's own crash-recovery scan instead"

> requirements.md REQ-002, closing paragraph: "Resolver Evidence (REQ-004) is
> still written on every Block, with **two** named exceptions:
> `disabled-legacy-invocation` ... and the self-referential
> `output-schema-validation-failed` case" — `artifact-publication-failed` is
> not among the exceptions; AC-012 repeats the rule per fixture.

> design.md, Crash-recovery scan: "a target's current live hash matches
> NEITHER its journal-recorded PRE nor POST value (an unrecoverable third
> state no automatic recovery can resolve) — this invocation does **not**
> proceed to step 1; Block, `publication-journal-recovery`, exit 1"

Writing the mandated Evidence necessarily produces the state the third clause
declares unrecoverable, so the first clause's promise cannot hold. Both
coordinator-suggested repairs (re-recording that target's hashes in the
retained journal, or dropping its entry) require AMENDING a retained journal
in place. The frozen contract defines exactly three journal operations — write
at Journal, delete at Complete, delete after a converged recovery — and no
amend. Adding a fourth journal operation on a `Security-Sensitive: true` task
is a contract change, so it is returned for human ruling.

**RULED 2026-08-27 — option (a), accepted as-is.** The conflict above was put
to the repository owner as a structured question, relayed via the coordinating
session, carrying both repair options: (a) accept the current fail-closed
behavior as a known limitation, or (b) authorize a fourth journal operation
(amend) / a design.md amendment. The owner selected (a), verbatim label:
「(a) 現行 fail-closed を既知制限として受容（推奨）」. The consequences, for a
future reviewer who meets this behavior cold: it is
SPECIFIED-WITH-A-KNOWN-LIMITATION, not an open defect; manual operator
intervention is by design in this doubly-degraded corner (a publication
failure AND a rollback that could not itself complete); no journal-amend
operation is authorized, and no design.md amendment follows. The corrected
wording below stands as the permanent record. The same ruling is recorded
in-situ in `_rollback_transaction`'s own docstring, so it is met at the point
of reading rather than only here.

What WAS done: the over-strong wording is corrected everywhere it appeared —
`_rollback_transaction`'s docstring now carries an explicit KNOWN LIMITATION
paragraph stating that the next scan Blocks for manual intervention rather
than converging, why (the two-mandate collision), and why the fix is a ruling
rather than a choice; `_rollback_clause` carries a note explaining that its
operator-facing sentence deliberately keeps REQ-002's wording verbatim rather
than diverging from the frozen text the limitation is about; and this report's
Summary/`Unresolved Items` are corrected. Behavior is unchanged and remains
fail-closed in every direction: no live bytes destroyed (PRE-images retained
on disk), no mixed generation left publishable, operator told explicitly.

### MINOR — orphaned staging directory on Prepare/Journal failure: **REAL, fixed**

Verified: `_rollback_transaction` returned early on `not journalled or count
== 0` without discarding the batch, so a Prepare-phase failure left a nonce
directory of pre-image backups behind. Because the scan only globs
`*/TRANSACTION.json`, a journal-less leftover is invisible to every later
invocation — it would accumulate forever. The early return now calls
`_discard_batch` whenever nothing reached a live path (which is exactly what a
later scan would do for an all-PRE journal, SAFE abandonment), covering both
the journalled and not-yet-journalled variants.

New scenario `artifact-publication-failed[prepare-phase]` makes the first
target a directory so Prepare fails before the journal exists, asserting no
staging debris — and incidentally covering the one `artifact-publication-failed`
rollback clause no fixture previously reached (the nothing-was-committed
variant).

## Panel Round 2 Remediation (2026-08-27)

Blind cross-model panel, round 2: anthropic PASSed (0 findings); openai found
two deeper security Majors on the containment surface round 1 introduced. Each
was verified against the frozen `security-spec.md` threat model before any
change. Dispositions: **MAJOR 1 real-but-out-of-scope (with citations, no code
change); MAJOR 2 verified-real-in-scope (fixed, TDD-first).**

### MAJOR 1 — PRE-image provenance / arbitrary content into an allowlisted target: **REAL, but OUT OF SCOPE per frozen threat model**

The finding is technically accurate: `_recover_journal` validates that a
journal's target paths are allowlisted (round 1) and that its self-declared
PRE/POST hashes are internally consistent, but it cannot authenticate the
PROVENANCE of the journal or its `pre/` backup bytes. A crafted MIX journal
can declare an allowlisted target's current bytes as POST and attacker-chosen
backup bytes as PRE, and recovery will "roll back" that target to the attacker
bytes. Self-declared hashes give integrity, not provenance. I reproduced the
mechanism mentally and it holds.

The coordinator's decision procedure asks: does the frozen threat model treat
the `.resolver-staging` area's CONTENT as attacker-authored, or does it trust
the single-writer staging area? I answer the latter — this is out of scope —
on four independent, citable grounds, and the answer is not ambiguous because
one of them makes the in-scope reading contradict the spec:

1. **Single-writer assumption, explicit deferral (design.md:1407-1419).** "This
   feature's Resolver assumes a single writer to a given `--feature` value's
   own Resolver-owned output paths ... A concurrent second invocation ... or a
   concurrent human/tool edit to the same live output paths outside this
   Resolver's own transactional commit, is **out of this feature's own scope (a
   future epic's own file-locking concern, Non-goals)**." A planted journal is
   exactly "a tool edit ... outside this Resolver's own transactional commit,"
   and the spec places that class out of scope.

2. **No consuming caller exists yet (security-spec.md:106, Authorization row).**
   "Future Gate/CI caller / a future Epic A6 consumer ... the caller's own
   enforcement path — **no live wiring exists yet (Non-goals)**." The exploit
   requires a later legitimate Resolver invocation to consume the planted
   journal in the real protected repo; the design states no such live
   invocation path exists, and the consumer is a future epic.

3. **The fix is cryptographically impossible within the frozen boundary
   (security-spec.md:132; requirements.md Security Boundaries).** "N/A — this
   feature ... defines no signing key, no HMAC, and carries no credential."
   Authenticating on-disk journal provenance against an adversary who can
   write the same disk REQUIRES a secret. The spec definitively excludes
   secrets/crypto. A requirement to authenticate journal provenance would
   therefore contradict the frozen no-crypto boundary — the spec cannot
   mandate the impossible, so the in-scope reading is not merely disfavored,
   it is self-contradictory. This is what makes the determination
   unambiguous rather than a judgment call I should STOP on.

4. **The clean line round 1 already drew, and the human accepted.** Round 1
   closed writes OUTSIDE the fixed named set — an absolute invariant
   (requirements.md:1144, "never ... writes outside" the named paths),
   independent of provenance. MAJOR 1 is the complement: attacker-chosen
   CONTENT written INTO an in-set target. Content-into-an-in-set-target is
   precisely what the single-writer assumption governs, and (1) places it out
   of scope. The staging area is classified as the Resolver's own "internal,
   transient publication-integrity artifact" (security-spec.md:116).

Determination: **real-but-out-of-scope-with-citation. No code change.** The
residual is a genuine limitation of a crypto-free, single-writer design and is
the future file-locking epic's concern. Note that round 1's allowlist already
caps the blast radius to the Resolver's OWN four output files — a planted
journal can corrupt the content of an allowlisted artifact but can no longer
escape the set (and MAJOR 2 below closes the symlinked-parent escape from that
same set). I did NOT guess: the no-crypto contradiction (ground 3) is
dispositive.

### MAJOR 2 — parent-directory symlink escape: **VERIFIED-REAL-IN-SCOPE, fixed**

This is the complement of MAJOR 1 and lands on the opposite side of the same
line: it is a write OUTSIDE the fixed named set, the exact invariant round 1
committed to (requirements.md:1144-1151) — reached through a mechanism round 1
left open. Round 1's `_normalized` is `os.path.normpath(os.path.abspath(...))`,
which collapses `..` but does not resolve symlinks; its own docstring justified
that by asserting the symlink case is "closed separately by the write
primitives themselves" (`os.replace` replaces a symlink AT THE TARGET). That
reasoning covers only a symlink at the FINAL component. A symlinked PARENT
(`generated/`, `specs/<feature>/`, or the staging dir) passes the lexical
allowlist while `mkdir`/`mkstemp`/`os.replace` follow it and write outside.

Crucially, this is NOT gated on the out-of-scope "plant a journal" capability:
it fires on the ORDINARY clean publication path (step 14) the first time a
Full-track resolve runs in a tree where `generated/` is a symlink — a
symlinked worktree, a relocated build dir, or a deliberately-planted one. So it
is also a plain correctness/containment bug, not only an adversarial one, which
is a second reason it is in scope where MAJOR 1 is not. And leaving it open
means round 1 did not actually deliver the "never writes outside the set"
invariant it claims — the lexical check is bypassable — so closing it completes
round 1's own accepted fix rather than adding a new requirement.

RED (`red-panel2-sh.log` / `red-panel2-ps1.log`, 323 passed / 4 failed, both
runtimes, captured against the pre-fix resolver in a scratch tree): the new
`publication-target-parent-symlink` fixture symlinks `generated/` to a sibling
directory holding a sentinel and runs a clean Full-track resolve. Against the
round-1 code the projection escaped — `outside-generated/project-context.resolved.json`
was overwritten with the real projection JSON — and the run returned `exit 0`
silently.

**Fix.** `_target_escapes_via_symlink(repo_root, feature, target)` resolves the
candidate the way the kernel will at write time (`os.path.realpath`, which
follows every ancestry symlink and, with `strict=False`, resolves the existing
prefix while leaving a not-yet-created leaf lexical) and requires the result to
be one of the fixed target locations in `_allowed_publication_targets_real` —
computed by resolving the TRUSTED BASES (`repo_root`, the script dir) once and
joining the fixed lexical subpath WITHOUT following further symlinks. Resolving
the base first is deliberate: on macOS `/var` is a symlink to `[PATH_REDACTED]
and every fixture temp repo lives under it, so a check that forbade any symlink
from the filesystem root down would reject every legitimate run; the threat is
a symlink INSIDE the controlled subtree, not one above the repository. The
check is wired into BOTH write surfaces — `_publish_bundle` (step 14, before
any live write; a hit raises `OSError` → `artifact-publication-failed`,
fail-closed before the journal exists) and `_recover_journal` (alongside the
round-1 lexical allowlist; a hit raises `PublicationJournalUnrecoverable` →
`publication-journal-recovery`). A companion check contains the staging batch
directory itself (`os.path.commonpath`) **on the publish path only** -- this
sentence originally claimed it meant "a symlinked `.resolver-staging` cannot
put the journal/backups outside `specs/<feature>/` either", which was true of
`_publish_bundle` and false of the crash-recovery scan; that asymmetry is the
panel-round-3 CRITICAL, corrected below. The realpath
check also subsumes the lexical `..`-traversal case, so the two checks are
belt-and-suspenders.

GREEN (`green-panel2-sh.log` / `green-panel2-ps1.log`): 327 passed / 0 failed,
both runtimes. The fixture asserts the Block (`artifact-publication-failed`
with the no-rollback clause), the byte-untouched outside sentinel, the
never-published Full-track artifact, the Block's own Resolver Evidence still
written (AC-012 — the Evidence write is direct, and it only ever touches
`resolver-evidence.yaml`, which `specs/<feature>/` still holds as a real
directory), and no journal/staging litter.

Mutation proof (private scratch tree — the shared scratchpad was again
overwritten by a concurrent agent mid-task): control `MUTATION[none] RESULT: 25
passed, 0 failed`; removing the publication-path parent-symlink check →
`MUTATION[g-no-parent-symlink-check] RESULT: 2 passed, 4 failed`, reproducing
the exploit exactly (projection escapes, `exit 0`).

## Panel Round 3 Remediation (2026-08-27)

Round 3 on bundle digest `3baa87a5`: both panelists independently found the
SAME defect on the recovery path, rated Major and CRITICAL respectively.
Disposition: **VERIFIED-REAL-IN-SCOPE, CRITICAL, fixed** — plus the two
overstated claims and two Minors the panelists flagged.

### CRITICAL — recovery-path staging containment: **VERIFIED REAL, fixed**

This is the mirror image of round 2's fix on the sibling code path that fix
did not reach: `_publish_bundle` validated that its batch directory resolves
inside `specs/<feature>/`, while `_crash_recovery_scan` validated neither the
staging root it globs nor the batch directory `_discard_batch` later deletes.
That asymmetry was mine, introduced in round 2.

**Why CRITICAL rather than Major**, and I confirmed this is the stronger
reading: the planted journal needs NO escaping target at all. One well-formed
entry naming an IN-SET, currently-ABSENT target (`pre_hash: "ABSENT"`)
classifies all-PRE / SAFE abandonment and reaches `_discard_batch` directly.
Round 1's allowlist and round 2's `_target_escapes_via_symlink` are both
consulted and both legitimately APPROVE — the target really is in-set. The
damage comes from the batch directory's own resolved location, which nothing
checked. All three converged outcomes (SAFE completion, SAFE abandonment, MIX)
funnel into `_discard_batch`, so all three reach the `rmtree`.

I verified the four mechanics empirically in isolation rather than trusting
the report: (1) `Path.glob` traverses a symlinked staging dir and returns the
journal beneath it; (2) `os.path.islink(batch_dir)` is False for the real
directory behind the symlink; (3) `shutil.rmtree` therefore does not refuse
and removes the external directory **and its contents**; (4)
`os.path.commonpath` raises `ValueError`, confirming Minor 2 below. With a
`.resolver-staging -> ../../..` symlink and a root `TRANSACTION.json` — both
ordinary committed files on a malicious branch, exactly the threat
`_recover_journal`'s own TRUST BOUNDARY comment already accepts — step 0.5
`rmtree`s the repository working tree.

**Scope.** In scope, on the same footing as round 2's MAJOR 2: a destructive
write OUTSIDE the fixed named path set (requirements.md:1144-1151, which
grants exactly one writable directory beyond the four output files — "its own
transient `specs/<feature>/.resolver-staging/` ... area"). It is NOT covered
by round 2's out-of-scope disposition (that one is attacker CONTENT written
INTO an in-set target, single-writer's domain) nor by the 2026-08-27
accept-as-is ruling (that one is the retained-journal/Evidence interaction).
Strictly worse than round 1's single-file unlink.

RED (`red-panel3-sh.log` / `red-panel3-ps1.log`, 329 passed / 6 failed, both
runtimes, captured against the pre-fix resolver): the external canary read
back `b'<MISSING>'` — recursively deleted — and the diagnostic was
misattributed to `artifact-publication-failed`.

**Fix — containment covers DISCOVERY as well as writes**, in three layers:

1. `_crash_recovery_scan` validates `_staging_area_contained(repo_root,
   feature)` **before the glob**, since discovery through the symlink is
   itself the first step of the exploit. Refuses having touched nothing.
2. `_recover_journal` re-validates each discovered journal's batch directory
   *and* the journal file itself against the resolved staging root — covering
   a nonce directory independently symlinked out of an otherwise-legitimate
   staging root, which layer 1 legitimately passes.
3. `_discard_batch` carries a self-contained guard (no repo/feature context
   needed, so it holds at every call site including cleanup paths). It
   precedes the `unlink`, not just the `rmtree`: `shutil.rmtree` refuses a
   symlink argument, but `journal.unlink()` would still follow one.

`_publish_bundle` was refactored onto the same shared helpers, so publish and
recovery are now provably governed by one containment rule instead of two
hand-maintained copies.

**Diagnostic id preserved.** A new `PublicationStagingAreaUncontained` keeps
the correct `publication-journal-recovery` id instead of letting the failure
degrade into a misattributed `artifact-publication-failed`.

**Corrected 2026-08-28 (round 10).** This paragraph used to end: "Because the
staging area a Block record's own single-target transaction would itself need
is precisely what is compromised, this path writes NOTHING." Both halves are
now false. The Evidence write needs no staging area — it is direct — so a
compromised staging area is no reason to withhold the Block record, and under
ruling B this path calls `_block` and writes Resolver Evidence on the
`publication-journal-recovery` id exactly as Main Workflows 4 specifies. The
only path that still writes nothing is the one where Evidence's own target
cannot be reached at all (`EvidenceTargetUncontained`), which is escalated
separately as a third AC-012 exception.
**Disclosed AC-012 interaction:** this is a second, no-write trigger of the
`publication-journal-recovery` row; the row's Evidence-writing behavior
remains covered by its original corruption fixture, which reaches the
diagnostic with an intact staging area.

**Fixture** `publication-staging-parent-symlink`, two scenarios:
`staging-root-symlinked` (the CRITICAL exploit, all-PRE/ABSENT journal) and
`nonce-dir-symlinked` (real staging root, symlinked nonce dir — the scenario
that proves layer 2). Each asserts the Block with the canonical line, the
external directory and both canaries intact, no live artifact, and no Evidence.

**Mutation proofs** (private scratch tree; control `MUTATION[none] RESULT: 48
passed, 0 failed`):

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| (h) pre-glob staging guard removed | 6 passed / **2 failed** |
| (j) `_recover_journal` batch-dir guard removed | 5 passed / **3 failed** |
| (i) `_discard_batch` self-guard removed | 23 passed / 0 failed |

**(i) killed nothing, and I am reporting that rather than hiding it.** Layers
1 and 2 catch both reachable scenarios first, so layer 3 is genuinely
unproven defense-in-depth against a case no fixture reaches. It is retained
deliberately — it is the only guard that holds if a future caller invokes
`_discard_batch` from a path that has not validated containment — but it
should not be counted as test-covered.

### Minor 2 — `commonpath` raises `ValueError`, not `OSError`: **REAL, fixed**

Confirmed empirically (mechanic 4 above). The round-2 guard called
`os.path.commonpath` inside a `try/except OSError`; on Windows a `subst`ed
drive or cross-drive junction raises `ValueError`, which would have escaped
`main()` as a raw traceback instead of the canonical `capability-resolver:
artifact-publication-failed:` line REQ-002/AC-014 require, bypassing
`_rollback_transaction` entirely. Unreachable on POSIX, but this file's `.ps1`
twin runs on Windows CI. Now centralized in `_path_contained_in`, which
catches `ValueError` and fails closed.

### Two overstated claims: **corrected**

1. The round-2 report sentence claiming the `commonpath` companion check meant
   "a symlinked `.resolver-staging` cannot put the journal/backups outside
   `specs/<feature>/` either" was true of `_publish_bundle` and false of the
   recovery scan — that asymmetry IS this round's CRITICAL. Sentence rewritten
   in place to say so.
2. `run_t007_parent_symlink_case`'s docstring named "or the staging dir" as
   part of the threat it exercised, when it only exercises `generated/` on the
   publish path. Corrected, with a pointer to the new recovery-path case.

### Minor 1 — Specification Differences item 2: **REAL, corrected**

The claim that "live state exactly as found" is honoured for "the journal's
own targets" was not strictly true: `_block` publishes
`resolver-evidence.yaml`, itself one of the four allowlisted targets a
retained journal may list, moving it off both PRE and POST and potentially
converting an operator-fixable batch into an unconvergeable one. The
AC-012-grounded decision to write Evidence is defensible and remains; the
over-broad phrasing is withdrawn in place.

## Panel Round 4 Remediation (2026-08-27)

Round 4 on bundle `35e4df22`: both vendors found the same defect (openai
Critical, anthropic Major — the split reflects blast radius, not disagreement
about the mechanism). Disposition: **VERIFIED REAL, IN SCOPE, fixed**, plus
four Minors closed in the same pass. This round named the ROOT of the class
rather than another instance, so it is written up as a design correction.

### Major — anchor drift in `_expected_staging_root_real`: **VERIFIED REAL, fixed**

`_expected_staging_root_real` built its reference as
`os.path.join(os.path.realpath(repo_root / "specs" / feature), STAGING_DIRNAME)`
— resolving `specs/<feature>`, an intermediate and branch-committable path
component, as though it were trusted. With `specs/` or `specs/<feature>`
symlinked out, the reference moved to the attacker's location, so
`_staging_area_contained` compared a realpath against a reference that had
resolved **the same symlink**. Both sides cancelled and the check passed
vacuously — the exact both-sides-resolve failure mode `_normalized`'s own
docstring warns about, reintroduced one layer up.

Verified directly against the staged resolver before changing anything:

```
Q1 _staging_area_contained  = True     <-- accepts an external staging tree
   _expected_staging_root_real = <tmp>/external-feature/.resolver-staging
```

**The exploit needs a specific journal shape, which is why no existing
scenario caught it.** A journal naming a target *under* the symlinked feature
dir is still refused by round 2's `_target_escapes_via_symlink`. The journal
must therefore name `generated/project-context.resolved.json` — a target
under the SCRIPT directory, genuinely where it belongs — so that round 1's
allowlist, round 2's target check, and round 3's staging/batch guards all
legitimately **approve**, the scan globs the external tree, and
`_discard_batch` `rmtree`s the external batch directory. RED
(`red-panel4-{sh,ps1}.log`, 337 passed / 2 failed both runtimes) confirms it:
`nonce_canary=b'<MISSING>' journal_exists=False`.

**Answer to the publish-path question, with evidence: NO, the publish path
does not have this hole.** In the same symlinked tree:

```
Q2 _target_escapes_via_symlink(facet-manifest) = True   <-- correctly refuses
   realpath(target)   = <tmp>/external-feature/facet-manifest.yaml
   allowed_real[..]   = <tmp>/repo/specs/example-feature/capability-summary.yaml
```

The two sides do **not** cancel, because `_allowed_publication_targets_real`
resolves only `repo_root` and then joins the fixed lexical subpath. This
refutes the first panelist's hypothesis that both sides would agree, and
confirms the second's: recovery-side only.

**The anchor.** `repo_root` is the one path in this program not derived from
repo-local, branch-committable metadata: `_find_repo_root` locates it by
walking up to a `.git`, and a `.git` component cannot be represented inside a
git tree, so no committed branch can plant or redirect it. The fix is
therefore a one-line correction, not a re-architecture — build the reference
from `os.path.realpath(repo_root)` plus the **whole fixed lexical subpath**,
matching `_allowed_publication_targets_real`. Layers 2 and 3 inherit a
trustworthy base automatically. My round-3 claim that publish and recovery are
"governed by one rule" was not yet true when written; it is true now.

### Four Minors, all closed

1. **`_expected_staging_root_real`'s docstring** asserted it used the "same
   trusted-base-then-fixed-subpath construction" as
   `_allowed_publication_targets_real`. Factually untrue as written, and
   actively misdirecting given the Standing Note points reviewers at these
   helpers. Rewritten alongside the code, naming the anchor explicitly.
2. **`_normalized`'s docstring** still carried the round-1 justification
   verbatim ("`os.replace` REPLACES a symlink at the target...") with no
   pointer to `_target_escapes_via_symlink`. True, but only for a FINAL-
   component symlink. Rewritten: symlinks are not this function's job, with
   explicit references to the three realpath-based checks that are.
3. **Layer-3 (`_discard_batch`) zero-kill justification** was overstated. The
   guard compares `realpath(batch_dir)` against `realpath(batch_dir.parent)`
   only, so it covers an escaping NONCE directory — not an escaping staging
   root or `specs/<feature>`, i.e. not this round's case. Comment corrected to
   state that scope precisely.
4. **Cleanup-after-refusal ordering.** The staging check raised `OSError`
   inside `_publish_bundle`'s `try`, so a refusal fell into the `except`
   handler → `_rollback_transaction` → `_discard_batch` →
   `batch_dir.parent.rmdir()`: an rmdir against the staging root just
   rejected. Harmless only by accident today (on POSIX the sole failing case
   was a symlinked `.resolver-staging`, and rmdir on a trailing symlink fails
   ENOTDIR, swallowed). The round-4 fix makes a real-directory staging root
   able to fail the check, which would have made it live. All pre-transaction
   validation is now extracted into `_validate_publication_preconditions`,
   called **outside** the `try` and raising `ArtifactPublicationFailed`
   directly, so "refused" and "cleaned up" are structurally disjoint.

## Panel Round 5 Remediation (2026-08-27)

Round 5 produced three items: one genuine implementation defect (anthropic
Major — FIXED), two documentation corrections (anthropic Minors — FIXED), and
two mutually-contradictory findings from openai that are **ESCALATED for human
ruling, not implemented** (see "Escalated: AC-047 / AC-012 collision" below).

### anthropic MAJOR — journal round-trip under an unresolved `repo_root`: **VERIFIED REAL, fixed**

The fifth instance of the containment class, with **inverted polarity**: a
FALSE REFUSAL (self-inflicted denial of service), not an escape. Four rounds of
escape-hunting missed it because every prior fixture asked "can an attacker get
OUT?" and this one asks "does the Resolver still accept its OWN journal?".

One live path was compared against three anchors: `_allowed_publication_targets`
mixed a raw-`repo_root` base (its `specs/<feature>` entries) with a
symlink-RESOLVED base (`Path(__file__).resolve().parent`, its `generated/`
entry); `_repo_relative` wrote journal paths relative to `repo_root.resolve()`;
`_journal_target_path` rebuilt them against the unresolved `repo_root`.
Verified directly before changing anything:

```
repo_root (as resolver holds it) = <tmp>/link-repo
realpath(repo_root)              = <tmp>/real-repo
journal live_path written  = plugins/.../generated/project-context.resolved.json
rebuilt by recovery        = <tmp>/link-repo/plugins/.../generated/...
allowlist entry            = <physical>/plugins/.../generated/...
ROUND-TRIP OK?             = False   <-- refuses its OWN journal
specs/<feature> entry OK?  = True    <-- round-trips by accident
```

`_find_repo_root` keeps the caller's lexical path verbatim for an absolute
`--config`, so this fires for any repository reached through a symlinked
ancestor — the ordinary case under macOS `/tmp` or `/var`, or any symlinked
checkout. Consequence: step 0.5 rejects a Full-track journal THIS RESOLVER
WROTE as "outside this feature's own fixed publication target set",
permanently, on every later invocation — contradicting REQ-002's own
`publication-journal-recovery` row ("a journal that *can* be safely converged
(the common case) is silently resolved by that same scan and never reaches
this diagnostic at all") and misattributing a self-authored artifact to the
attack condition round 1's allowlist exists to catch. Fail-closed (PRE-images
retained, no live bytes destroyed), hence Major.

**Why the existing suite could not see it, and what the new fixture does
differently.** Every other T-007 fixture builds its repo as
`Path(tmp).resolve()` and drives a RELATIVE `--config`, so `repo_root` is
already physical and all three anchors coincide — including round 4's
`feature-dir-symlinked` scenario, whose journal names exactly this target and
RELIES on the allowlist approving it. The new case
`publication-journal-roundtrip-unresolved-repo` therefore drives an ABSOLUTE
`--config` through a symlinked ancestor (`<tmp>/link-repo -> <tmp>/real-repo`),
crashes a real Full-track publish via the kill hook to leave a genuine,
resolver-authored journal, and asserts the next invocation converges it
SILENTLY (no `publication-journal-recovery`, exit 0, journal deleted).

**Fix:** resolve the anchor exactly once, in `main()` —
`repo_root = Path(os.path.realpath(str(_find_repo_root(absolute_config))))` —
so all three anchors coincide by construction. This is the Standing Note's own
rule applied to the anchor itself; it weakens nothing (the anchor is the
`.git`-bearing directory, which committed content cannot redirect) and
resolves no intermediate component anywhere.

### anthropic MINOR 1 — layer 2 was not independent: **VERIFIED REAL, fixed**

`_recover_journal` built `staging_real` as
`os.path.realpath(str(_staging_root(repo_root, feature)))` — a RESOLVED
INTERMEDIATE, the exact construction the Standing Note forbids, so for the
symlinked-staging-root case both sides cancelled and the layer silently
depended on layer 1 having run first. Round 3's own mutation (h) was the
evidence: removing layer 1 failed 2 tests, which is only possible if layer 2
does not catch what layer 1 catches. Now
`_expected_staging_root_real(repo_root, feature)`, making the layer genuinely
independent, so "one containment rule governs both paths" holds by
construction rather than by call ordering.

### anthropic MINOR 2 — emitted-vs-expected corrected IN CODE: **VERIFIED REAL, fixed**

The round-1 comment-level finding was corrected only in report prose. Both
in-code descriptions still claimed emitted-not-expected —
`Counts.__init__`'s comment ("ids this run actually OBSERVED a fixture Block
with") and `run_block_matrix_completeness_check`'s docstring ("ids the fixtures
above ACTUALLY produced a canonical diagnostic line for"). `record_diagnostic_id`
takes each case's hardcoded `expected_id` unconditionally, beside (not after)
the canonical-line assertion. Both rewritten in place to describe a COVERAGE
check and to name where emitted-vs-expected is actually enforced. A reviewer
now meets the accurate description where they read the mechanism.
